problem: "The tangential force Ft acts near the pitch point" is wrong and contradicts the lead and the quiz answer. Lewis puts the whole load at the tooth tip (one tooth carrying everything), because that gives the largest bending moment at the root. The pitch point is not the worst case.
fix: "The tangential force Ft acts at the tooth tip — the worst case, with one tooth taking the whole load — and the root fillet is the fixed end."

where: Section 1, second paragraph ('An equivalent form is σb b πm Y, with Y = πy'), repeated in Exam trap 4
problem: The relation between the two forms of the Lewis equation is inverted. From σb b m y = σb b π m Y it follows that Y = y/π, not πy. As written, σb b π m (πy) = π² σb b m y, about 9.9 times too large. With y = 0.32, the π-form factor must be about 0.10, not 1.0.
fix: "An equivalent form is Ft = σb b π m y′, where y′ = y/π (about 0.102 when y = 0.32). Books that put π inside the formula tabulate this smaller factor; the two tabulated factors differ by the factor π. Use one form only." In trap 4 write: "y and y′ are not the same: with the π inside the formula the factor is y/π, roughly a third of the other."

where: Section 2 last paragraph, Section 3 design order, Exam trap 5
problem: The bending check compares the static force Ft with the beam strength, while the wear check uses the dynamic load Fd. Section 2 itself says "the dynamic load is what the tooth actually feels", so leaving it out of bending is inconsistent and understates the bending load. Standard treatments compare the dynamic (effective) load with both limits.
fix: "Two checks close the design: Fd ≤ beam strength (σb b m y) and Fd ≤ Fw. Lewis sizing with Ft is only a first pass." In trap 5: "beam strength and wear load are both compared with the dynamic load Fd; the static Ft only gives the first size."

problem: "a small tooth has a stubbier, more highly stressed root" is misleading. A stubby tooth is stronger. With fewer teeth the involute flank is more sharply curved and the root is relatively thin, and below about 17 teeth a 20° full-depth tooth is undercut.
fix: "y falls as the tooth count falls, because with fewer teeth the flanks are more sharply curved and the root is relatively thin (undercut below about 17 teeth), so the same load bends the tooth more."

problem: Most Indian textbooks use a velocity factor Cv less than 1 and divide: effective load = Ft/Cv. The factor greater than 1 that multiplies is the AGMA/Shigley dynamic factor Kv. A student will use the wrong symbol direction. The sentence "Do not apply Cv and Fd without knowing which method your syllabus uses" is also unclear.
fix: "Two conventions exist. The AGMA/Shigley dynamic factor Kv is greater than 1: Ft,eff = Kv Ft. The velocity factor Cv in many Indian textbooks is less than 1: Ft,eff = Ft/Cv. Use one convention only; never apply both the velocity factor and the Buckingham Fd in the same check."

problem: "Forgetting v, or forgetting the velocity factor Cv, gives a force that is too low" does not say what error is meant; leaving v out of Ft = P/v does not by itself give a force that is too low.
fix: "Using d1 in millimetres instead of metres inside v = πd1n/60 makes v 1000 times too large and Ft 1000 times too small. Always put d1 in metres when v must come out in m/s."
